transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Rajiv Menon: Rajiv here, CTO, Halo Systems.
[00:09] Sophie Park: Sophie, ML eng on the inference team.
[00:11] Daniel Ruiz: Daniel, infra. Glad to get into this.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Great. Liam are you with us?
[00:16] Liam Patel: Yep Liam Patel, Redwood SE. I'll drive the deep dive.
[00:19] Maya Chen: Perfect, goal today is to understand the KV cache evictions you've been seeing under long sessions, paging behavior, and whether prefix reuse is causing churn. We'll also cover batching and quantization impacts and any VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:33] Sophie Park: Quick context — we run a chat product where sessions go up to ~40k tokens and we saw sudden latency spikes and some 5xx errors last week. We suspect evictions, maybe paging, but not sure if it's our prompt patterns or model config.
[00:48] Liam Patel: Okay. Do you have traced metrics — cache hit rate, evict counts, memory pressure events?
[00:52] Sophie Park: We exported some dashboards. Hit rate hovers 82-88% but evictions jump in bursts around heavy multi-session windows. We also saw paging activity on the node that hosts cold prefixes.
[01:04] Liam Patel: Interesting. A few hypotheses — first, prefix reuse can cause very large KV entries if you have many unique conversation prefixes and limited per-GPU KV allocation. Second, quantized models change the per-token KV footprint a bit but mostly affect compute; third, batching combined with uneven sequence lengths can push memory pressure transiently.
[01:23] Rajiv Menon: For us, prefix reuse comes from session templates — lots of similar intros but each user adds a handful of metadata tokens so prefixes are similar but not identical. Might be high cardinality.
[01:36] Liam Patel: That drives the cardinality problem. If the runtime keys are keyed per-prefix-and-session you get many cache entries that never see reuse. Eviction policy default is LRU-ish with size-based heuristics; if many near-unique prefixes come in, you'll evict older useful KV shards.
[01:50] Daniel Ruiz: We also run with quantized 4-bit weights for cost; any interactions there?
[01:53] Liam Patel: Quantization changes the model memory but the KV cache is mostly activations and past key/values. For some kernels, quantized execution paths use slightly different packing which can change the on-device transient memory use; that can exacerbate paging if the device memory is tight. Not a huge change in steady-state KV footprint but affects peak.
[02:11] Sophie Park: We also noticed batch sizes varied a lot — autoscaling lists show bursts where batch size doubled for 30s. Could that cause eviction cascades?
[02:18] Liam Patel: Yes. Continuous batching is great for throughput, but if you get many long sequences in a single batch, the runtime may allocate additional KV buffers for the longer context, bumping memory and causing eviction. We often recommend workload-aware batching caps and per-route max_sequence settings.
[02:34] Maya Chen: To add, our Intelligent batching heuristics try to bound worst-case token allocation; if your workload has high variance, set conservative max_seq or enable prefix compaction.
[02:42] Rajiv Menon: Prefix compaction?
[02:44] Liam Patel: It's a feature where similar prefixes can be hashed into reuse buckets — it reduces cardinality at the cost of some cache misses when prefixes differ in meaningful ways. Good for template-heavy workloads.
[02:55] Sophie Park: Might be acceptable; accuracy loss from compaction — how often do we see semantic regressions?
[02:59] Liam Patel: Usually low, but depends on how semantics are encoded in the differing tokens. We can run an eval set to measure quality regression. We also suggested quantization-aware KV diagnostics to ensure packing isn't introducing artifacts.
[03:12] Daniel Ruiz: You mentioned paging — are we talking GPU eviction to CPU or OS-level swapping?
[03:17] Liam Patel: Two types: device-level paging (e.g., GPU memory oversubscription / MIG swapping) and runtime-managed spilling to CPU RAM in our paging mode. Device-level OOM leads to hard failures; runtime spilling is slower but keeps the process alive. We saw in your logs some runtime spill events.
[03:31] Rajiv Menon: Those correlate with the 5xx spikes.
[03:34] Liam Patel: Exactly. Spilling increases latency dramatically for those affected requests. The right fix is reducing peak memory footprint or enlarging KV allocation per GPU or tuning the eviction threshold.
[03:44] Sophie Park: Can we increase per-GPU KV allocation? We're on a medium Dedicated pool now.
[03:49] Liam Patel: Yes if you move to a larger instance class or reserve extra KV memory via Dedicated config. There's also a config knob to reserve more headroom for long-context sessions. Tradeoff is less capacity per GPU -> higher cost.
[04:02] Maya Chen: We can model that tradeoff — provide Throughput vs Cost sheet.
[04:06] Sophie Park: Another observed behavior: prefix reuse seems to sometimes amplify — we see one prefix used in many sessions but with slight trailing tokens. The cache stores separate entries and doesn't dedupe. Is there dedupe?
[04:19] Liam Patel: Not automatically at the granularity you describe. If the trailing tokens change the key, it treats them as distinct entries. We have prefix normalization features and canonicalization to map near-identical prefixes to a canonical form; that's similar to compaction but more controlled.
[04:35] Daniel Ruiz: Is canonicalization safe for PII-sensitive tokens? We can't canonicalize away user IDs if those influence responses.
[04:42] Liam Patel: Right, you should exclude or mask PII before canonicalization. We support pre-processing hooks where you can mask tokens in metadata while preserving semantic context.
[04:53] Sophie Park: About telemetry — what exact logs do you need to reproduce? We can send some traces.
[04:58] Liam Patel: Send per-request KV hit/miss, eviction events with timestamps, memory pressure events, and the request token lengths. If you can correlate request IDs to the 5xx traces that's ideal. Also send a representative set of prompts with growth patterns.
[05:12] Maya Chen: We'll include an example command and the preferred format in the runbook.
[05:16] Rajiv Menon: Security question — if we move to Private deployment in our VPC, do we still get the same KV diagnostics? Concerned about logs in S3 and encryption.
[05:25] Liam Patel: Yes, Private supports the full telemetry stack. We integrate with your KMS for encryption at rest; audit logs can be delivered to your S3 bucket or internal SIEM. For VPC we use a control-plane-to-data-plane cert mechanism; logs can be configured to remain in your environment.
[05:40] Daniel Ruiz: And about KMS keys — can we bring our own HSM-backed keys?
[05:44] Maya Chen: We support BYOK via cloud KMS integrations and HSM for enterprise Private customers; it'll require slightly different onboarding.
[05:50] Sophie Park: Back to batching — any best-practice numbers for batch caps and dynamic bucketing?
[05:56] Liam Patel: We typically recommend a per-route max_batch_tokens threshold and a batch depth cap for long-context routes. Example: cap at 4096 tokens per batch or use adaptive batching where very long sequences go to a priority lane. That reduces head-of-line blocking and memory spikes.
[06:12] Rajiv Menon: What about tokenization differences and KV size? We use a custom tokenizer with ~1.2x token count compared to standard; could that explain more memory?
[06:21] Liam Patel: Absolutely — more tokens -> more KV entries. Effective context is higher. We can account for that in the config by scaling the expected KV per-token parameter.
[06:30] Sophie Park: Any interactions with attention optimizations? We use rotary embeddings and some trimmed attention kernels.
[06:36] Liam Patel: Some kernels use fused attention that reduces temporary buffers; others use KV-packed formats. If your model uses custom ops, kernel selection might suboptimally allocate extra scratch memory. We can provide a kernel profile to see which execution path is taken.
[06:50] Daniel Ruiz: There's also a question about eviction policy — can we change from LRU to size-aware or MRU for specific workloads?
[06:57] Liam Patel: You can tune eviction policy and set per-route priorities. For instance, mark system-critical prefixes as protected so they avoid eviction. There's also tiered cache — sticky hot entries vs ephemeral.
[07:10] Maya Chen: To test, we'll propose two experiments: a) enable prefix canonicalization + conservative batching and run for 24h; b) keep current config but increase KV allocation on a single node and compare tail latency.
[07:22] Sophie Park: That sounds good. How do we measure success?
[07:25] Liam Patel: Primary metrics: 99th percentile latency, frequency of spill events, eviction rate, and model output quality (via your eval set to detect regressions). Aim to reduce spill-induced 5xx to zero in the pilot window and keep output quality within X% of baseline.
[07:39] Rajiv Menon: What's the expected cost delta for increasing KV allocation? Ballpark.
[07:43] Maya Chen: We'll run the numbers but typically moving one tier up increases node cost ~25-40% while increasing effective capacity by ~60-80% depending on model. We'll share a throughput vs cost sheet.
[07:55] Daniel Ruiz: One more — can cache eviction be instrumented for alerting? We want proactive alarms before spills.
[08:00] Liam Patel: Yes, set thresholds for memory pressure and eviction rates; we can hook alerts to PagerDuty. We also have regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[08:09] Sophie Park: Any gotchas with long-context debugging? We had some transcripts that seemed truncated in our logs.
[08:15] Liam Patel: That could be due to sampling in your logging or retention windows. For long sessions, ensure you set full-trace capture for debug windows. We'll include guidance.
[08:26] Maya Chen: Okay wrapping up — quick recap: Liam will send eviction histograms and a runbook; Maya will send cost/throughput worksheet and pilot terms; Sophie/Daniel will send logs and traces. We'll schedule a 30-minute benchmark next week.
[08:40] Rajiv Menon: Agreed.
[08:42] Sophie Park: Thanks everyone.
[08:44] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links.
[08:48] Liam Patel: Thanks — will attach sample queries and config diffs.
[08:52] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]
